q1.text: But he, Siddhartha, was not a source of joy for himself, he found no delight in himself. Walking the rosy paths of the fig tree garden, sitting in the bluish shade of the grove of contemplation, washing his limbs daily in the bath of repentance, sacrificing in the dim shade of the mango forest, his gestures of perfect decency, everyone's love and joy, he still lacked all joy in his heart. Dreams and restless thoughts came into his mind, flowing from the water of the river, sparkling from the stars of the night, melting from the beams of the sun, dreams came to him and a restlessness of the soul, fuming from the sacrifices, breathing forth from the verses of the Rig-Veda, being infused into him, drop by drop, from the teachings of the old Brahmins.

q2.text: But more than all the others he was loved by Govinda, his friend, the son of a Brahmin. He loved Siddhartha's eye and sweet voice, he loved his walk and the perfect decency of his movements, he loved everything Siddhartha did and said and what he loved most was his spirit, his transcendent, fiery thoughts, his ardent will, his high calling. Govinda knew: he would not become a common Brahmin, not a lazy official in charge of offerings; not a greedy merchant with magic spells; not a vain, vacuous speaker; not a mean, deceitful priest; and also not a decent, stupid sheep in the herd of the many.

q3.text: Often he spoke to himself from a Chandogya-Upanishad the words: "Truly, the name of the Brahman is satyam—verily, he who knows such a thing, will enter the heavenly world every day." Often, it seemed near, the heavenly world, but never had he reached it completely, never had he quenched the ultimate thirst. And among all the wise and wisest men, he knew and whose instructions had he received, among all of them there was no one, who had reached it completely, the heavenly world, who had quenched it completely, the eternal thirst.

q4.text: Once, Samanas had travelled through Siddhartha's town, ascetics on a pilgrimage, three skinny, withered men, neither old nor young, with dusty and bloody shoulders, almost naked, scorched by the sun, surrounded by loneliness, strangers and enemies to the world, strangers and lank jackals in the realm of humans. Behind them blew a hot scent of quiet passion, of destructive service, of merciless self-denial.

q5.text: The Brahmin fell silent, and remained silent for so long that the stars in the small window wandered and changed their relative positions, ere the silence was broken. Silent and motionless stood the son with his arms folded, silent and motionless sat the father on the mat, and the stars traced their paths in the sky. Then spoke the father: "Not proper it is for a Brahmin to speak harsh and angry words. But indignation is in my heart. I wish not to hear this request for a second time from your mouth."

q6.text: After an hour, since no sleep had come over his eyes, the Brahmin stood up, paced to and fro, and left the house. Through the small window of the chamber he looked back inside, and there he saw Siddhartha standing, his arms folded, not moving from his spot. Pale shimmered his bright robe. With anxiety in his heart, the father returned to his bed. After another hour, since no sleep had come over his eyes, the Brahmin stood up again, paced to and fro, walked out of the house and saw that the moon had risen. Through the window of the chamber he looked back inside; there stood Siddhartha, not moving from his spot, his arms folded, moonlight reflecting from his bare shins. With worry in his heart, the father went back to bed.

q7.text: The first light of day shone into the room. The Brahmin saw that Siddhartha was trembling softly in his knees. In Siddhartha's face he saw no trembling, his eyes were fixed on a distant spot. Then his father realized that even now Siddhartha no longer dwelt with him in his home, that he had already left him. The Father touched Siddhartha's shoulder. "You will," he spoke, "go into the forest and be a Samana. When you'll have found blissfulness in the forest, then come back and teach me to be blissful. If you'll find disappointment, then return and let us once again make offerings to the gods together. Go now and kiss your mother, tell her where you are going to. But for me it is time to go to the river and to perform the first ablution."

q8.text: Govinda turned pale, when he heard these words and read the decision in the motionless face of his friend, unstoppable like the arrow shot from the bow. Soon and with the first glance, Govinda realized: Now it is beginning, now Siddhartha is taking his own way, now his fate is beginning to sprout, and with his, my own. And he turned pale like a dry banana skin.

q9.text: Siddhartha knew many venerable Brahmins, chiefly his father, the pure one, the scholar, the most venerable one. His father was to be admired, quiet and noble were his manners, pure his life, wise his words, delicate and noble thoughts lived behind its brow—but even he, who knew so much, did he live in blissfulness, did he have peace, was he not also just a searching man, a thirsty man?

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha is troubled because his friends and family no longer love him.
Though everyone delights in Siddhartha, he finds no joy in himself.
Siddhartha delights in the daily rituals of the grove and the river bath.
Siddhartha finds joy only in the verses of the Rig-Veda.
A.explanation: The passage turns on a contrast: amid "everyone's love and joy, he still lacked all joy in his heart." He performs the rituals but they bring restlessness, not delight. His family and friends still love him; that love is what fails to satisfy. The Rig-Veda verses feed his restlessness rather than his joy.

A.prompt: According to the passage, how long did the Brahmin remain silent?
options: Until his wife called him to the evening offering
So long that the stars in the window changed positions
Only for a moment before he answered calmly
Until Govinda came into the chamber to speak
A.explanation: The passage says he was silent "so long that the stars in the small window wandered and changed their relative positions." That rules out a moment's pause and a calm answer; his reply is indignant. Govinda does not enter the chamber here. No call from his wife or an evening offering interrupts the silence.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "anxiety" most nearly means
options: worry
eagerness
sleepiness
anger
A.explanation: The father returns to bed "with anxiety in his heart," and the next paragraph repeats the idea as "with worry in his heart," so worry fits. Anger appears elsewhere in the chapter but is not this word's sense. Sleepiness is wrong, since no sleep comes to him. Eagerness is a hopeful feeling, unlike his unease.

options: plans to stop Siddhartha by telling his father at once
believes his own future is bound to Siddhartha's decision
is relieved that Siddhartha will finally leave him behind
thinks the decision is only a passing whim
A.explanation: Govinda realizes "now his fate is beginning to sprout, and with his, my own," so he sees his future tied to Siddhartha's choice. Turning pale shows fear, not relief. Nothing suggests he plans to tell the father. He reads a decision "unstoppable like the arrow," so he does not think it a passing whim.

A.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the father decide?
options: To send Govinda to bring Siddhartha back from the forest
To keep Siddhartha at home until he gives up his plan
To let Siddhartha go to the forest and become a Samana
To go with Siddhartha to the forest and live as an ascetic
A.explanation: The father gives way and grants permission. He does not keep his son home; he sends him to kiss his mother goodbye. He himself goes "to the river" for the ablution, not to the forest. Govinda is never mentioned in the father's words here.

A.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "In Siddhartha's face he saw no trembling, his eyes were fixed on a distant spot."
"The first light of day shone into the room."
"You will," he spoke, "go into the forest and be a Samana."
"But for me it is time to go to the river and to perform the first ablution."
A.explanation: Only "You will... go into the forest and be a Samana" states the father's decision. The first light of day sets the time but decides nothing. The steady face is what the father notices before deciding, not the decision. Going to the river for the ablution is the father's own duty, not his ruling about his son.

A.prompt: The series of phrases beginning "not a" mainly serves to
options: describe the jobs Siddhartha's father hopes he will one day take up
name the teachers who have taught Siddhartha in the town
show that Govinda himself is a lazy and deceitful priest
list the ordinary roles Govinda is sure Siddhartha will never fill
A.explanation: Each "not a" names a common type, the lazy official, greedy merchant, vain speaker, to show what Govinda "knew" Siddhartha would never become. These are not his father's hopes, which are for a great wise man and priest. They are types, not named teachers. They describe Siddhartha, not Govinda himself.

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: The moon rises and the father decides to perform his evening prayers.
The father sleeps soundly once he has refused his son's request firmly and calmly.
Siddhartha leaves the house during the night while his father sleeps.
The father keeps rising in the night to find his son still standing there.
A.explanation: Both paragraphs show the father rising, "since no sleep had come over his eyes," and seeing Siddhartha "not moving from his spot," so the main idea is his repeated checking. He does not sleep soundly. Siddhartha stays in the chamber rather than leaving. The moon rising is a detail; no prayers are described.

A.prompt: According to the passage, how often had Siddhartha reached the heavenly world completely?
options: Never, though it often seemed near
Every day, as the verse promised
Many times, with the help of the wise men
Once, during his deepest meditation
A.explanation: The passage says "never had he reached it completely," though "often, it seemed near." The verse promises the heavenly world "every day," but he has not found that. No single success during meditation is mentioned. The wise men did not help, since "there was no one, who had reached it completely."

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "withered" most nearly means
options: dried up and shrunken
proud
bent with old age
frightened
A.explanation: The Samanas are "skinny, withered men," "scorched by the sun," so the sense is dried up and shrunken. "Bent with old age" fails because they are "neither old nor young." Nothing shows them frightened; they are strangers and enemies to the world. "Proud" describes an attitude, while withered here describes their bodies.

A.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha has begun to
options: lose all respect for his father and for all the other Brahmins
believe that his father has reached the Atman
wish to become a teacher of the holy books himself
doubt whether even his admired father has found peace
A.explanation: After praising his father, Siddhartha asks whether he did "live in blissfulness" or was "just a searching man, a thirsty man," showing doubt about his peace. He still admires his father ("to be admired"), so he has not lost respect. The questions deny rather than affirm that his father has reached the Atman. Teaching the books is not mentioned.

A.prompt: The comparison "pale like a dry banana skin" mainly emphasises
options: how hungry Govinda had become after the meditation under the banyan tree
how angry Govinda was at being left out
how suddenly fear drained the colour from Govinda's face
how old Govinda looked beside his friend
A.explanation: The simile follows Govinda's shock at Siddhartha's decision, so it stresses fear draining his colour. Hunger is not mentioned in the passage. He is a young man, and the image concerns colour, not age. He turns pale from fear and submission, not anger; Siddhartha sees fear in his soul.

B.prompt: According to the passage, what does the father ask Siddhartha to do if he finds blissfulness in the forest?
options: Stay in the forest and never return home
Send word to his mother through Govinda
Come back and teach him to be blissful
Bring the Samanas back to the town with him
B.explanation: The father says, "When you'll have found blissfulness in the forest, then come back and teach me to be blissful." He does not ask him to stay away forever. Sending word through Govinda is not mentioned. Bringing the Samanas to town is not part of his request; he speaks only of his son's return.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "venerable" most nearly means
options: deserving deep respect
strict
very old
wealthy
B.explanation: Siddhartha's father is "the most venerable one," "to be admired," with "quiet and noble" manners, so the word means deserving deep respect. "Very old" is a common association but the passage praises his worth, not his age. Nothing shows him strict. Wealth is never mentioned; his purity and wisdom are what is praised.

B.prompt: The father's behaviour in the passage suggests that he
options: is pleased with his son's stubbornness and proud of him
plans to punish Siddhartha harshly in the morning
is deeply troubled but unwilling to drag his son away by force
has already forgotten his son's request and sleeps peacefully until dawn
B.explanation: He rises again and again, looks in, and returns to bed with "anxiety" and "worry," yet never enters to remove his son, so he is troubled but does not use force. He cannot sleep, so he has not forgotten. Anxiety and worry are not pride. No plan to punish is suggested; his feelings are worry, not vengeance.

B.prompt: Based on the passage, what did Govinda know about Siddhartha?
options: He would remain in his father's house.
He would ask Govinda to lead him.
He would soon become a wealthy merchant in town.
He would not become an ordinary Brahmin.
B.explanation: The passage says "Govinda knew: he would not become a common Brahmin," followed by other ordinary roles he would avoid. Becoming a merchant is one of the roles he would not take. Remaining at home is not what Govinda foresees; he expects a "high calling." Govinda wants to follow, not lead, so asking Govinda to lead reverses it.

B.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "He loved Siddhartha's eye and sweet voice, he loved his walk"
"he would not become a common Brahmin, not a lazy official in charge of offerings"
"But more than all the others he was loved by Govinda, his friend, the son of a Brahmin."
"he loved everything Siddhartha did and said"
B.explanation: Only the line "he would not become a common Brahmin" states what Govinda knew about Siddhartha's future. The lines about Siddhartha's eye and voice show Govinda's love, not his knowledge. "More than all the others" says who loved him most. "He loved everything Siddhartha did" shows devotion, not foresight.

B.prompt: The detail about the stars that "traced their paths in the sky" mainly serves to
options: describe the beauty of the night outside the town
show that Siddhartha wishes to travel by night
suggest that the father is reading omens in the sky through the small window
show how much time passes while father and son stay silent
B.explanation: The stars wander "ere the silence was broken" and keep tracing their paths while both stand "silent and motionless," marking time passing. No one reads omens; the stars measure the silence. The beauty of the night is not the point of this tense scene. Siddhartha stands still with folded arms, so no night journey is suggested.

B.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha had reached the heavenly world through repeating the verse.
No one Siddhartha knew had fully reached the heavenly world he sought.
Siddhartha had stopped wishing to reach the heavenly world.
The wise men had shown Siddhartha the way to the heavenly world.
B.explanation: The passage says he never reached it completely and that among the wisest men "there was no one, who had reached it completely." Repeating the verse did not get him there. The wise men lacked it themselves, so they could not show the way. He still thirsts, so he has not stopped wishing.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "lank" most nearly means
options: loyal
swift
thin and bony
lazy
B.explanation: The Samanas are "three skinny, withered men," and the phrase "lank jackals" continues the picture of thin, starved bodies. "Lazy" does not fit men of "destructive service" and "merciless self-denial." "Swift" describes speed, which is not mentioned. "Loyal" is a dog-like trait, but jackals here suggest hunger and wildness, not loyalty.

B.prompt: The repeated phrase "since no sleep had come over his eyes" mainly serves to
options: introduce a new character into the scene outside the house
show the same sleepless round happening again and again
explain why Siddhartha is trembling in the morning
show that the father has decided to give in
B.explanation: The phrase opens both paragraphs, so the night repeats: rise, pace, look in, return. No new character enters. Siddhartha's trembling is described later, not explained by the father's sleeplessness. The repeated phrase shows his worry continuing, not a decision to give in, which comes only at dawn.

B.prompt: The passage suggests that the love of others
options: makes Siddhartha proud and careless in his duties
is the main source of Siddhartha's happiness
is something Siddhartha has never received
cannot fill the emptiness Siddhartha feels within
B.explanation: He is surrounded by "everyone's love and joy" yet "lacked all joy in his heart," so others' love cannot fill his emptiness. It is not the source of his happiness, since he has none. He performs his duties with "perfect decency," not carelessness. He receives much love, so "never received" is false.

B.prompt: The questions near the end of the passage mainly present
options: Siddhartha's private doubts about his father's peace of mind
a conversation between Siddhartha and his father
the father's own complaints about the Brahmins
Govinda's opinion of Siddhartha's father
B.explanation: The questions ("did he live in blissfulness, did he have peace") come from Siddhartha's mind, presenting his private doubts. No one speaks aloud, so it is not a conversation. The father does not complain; he is the subject of the questions. Govinda does not appear in this passage.

B.prompt: How does the father's attitude in Passage 2 differ from his attitude in Passage 1?
options: He moves from refusing the request to granting it.
He is angry in both passages and never changes.
He moves from granting the request to refusing it.
He ignores his son in both passages.
B.explanation: In Passage 1 he says he wishes "not to hear this request for a second time"; in Passage 2 he tells his son, "You will... go into the forest." So he moves from refusal to permission. The reverse order is wrong. He touches his son's shoulder in Passage 2, so he is not angry throughout or ignoring him.

C.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha gives up his plan to please his father at dawn.
Seeing that his son has already left him in spirit, the father lets him go.
Seeing his son tremble, the father decides that he must stay home with him forever.
The father leaves the house in anger and refuses to say goodbye.
C.explanation: The father realizes "Siddhartha no longer dwelt with him in his home," then grants permission, so the key fits. The trembling knees do not lead him to keep his son home. He touches his son's shoulder and gives instructions, so he does not leave in anger. Siddhartha does not give up; he goes to his mother as told.

C.prompt: The passage most strongly suggests that Siddhartha's teachers
options: had warned him never to repeat the verse
had already reached the heavenly world long ago
were themselves still thirsting for what he sought
had kept the path to the heavenly world secret from him
C.explanation: Among "all the wise and wisest men" no one "had quenched it completely, the eternal thirst," so they too still thirsted. Nothing suggests they kept a secret; they simply lacked it. No warning about the verse is mentioned. The passage denies that any had reached the heavenly world completely.

C.prompt: The repetition of "now" in Govinda's realization mainly serves to
options: suggest that Govinda doubts Siddhartha's words
convey a sense that fate is beginning to unfold at this moment
contrast the present with Govinda's happy childhood
show that Govinda is impatient to leave at once
C.explanation: "Now it is beginning, now Siddhartha is taking his own way, now his fate is beginning to sprout" piles up the present moment, conveying fate unfolding. Govinda turns pale, so he is not impatient. No childhood memory is contrasted. He reads the decision as unstoppable, so he does not doubt it.

C.prompt: What does Siddhartha conclude about his father in the passage?
options: His father has stopped making offerings and reading the books.
His father has found the peace that he himself is seeking.
Even his father may still be searching for what he lacks.
His father is a foolish man whose words are not wise.
C.explanation: His questions end with "was he not also just a searching man, a thirsty man?" suggesting his father still searches. That rules out the father having found peace. He calls his father wise ("wise his words"), not foolish. The father still seeks wisdom from offerings and books, so he has not stopped.

C.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "Siddhartha knew many venerable Brahmins, chiefly his father"
"pure his life, wise his words, delicate and noble thoughts lived behind its brow"
"His father was to be admired, quiet and noble were his manners"
"was he not also just a searching man, a thirsty man?"
C.explanation: Only "was he not also just a searching man, a thirsty man?" voices the conclusion that his father may still be searching. The lines praising his manners, purity and wise words show admiration, not doubt. "Siddhartha knew many venerable Brahmins" introduces the father but does not judge whether he has found peace.

C.prompt: As used in the passage, "infused" most nearly means
options: set on fire
frozen solid
instilled little by little
cleaned thoroughly with water
C.explanation: Restlessness is "being infused into him, drop by drop, from the teachings," so it is instilled gradually. "Cleaned" fits the bath of repentance, but not this word. "Set on fire" echoes "fuming from the sacrifices," yet infusing means pouring in. "Frozen" has no support in the passage.

C.prompt: The phrase "drop by drop" suggests that Siddhartha's restlessness
options: built up slowly over a long time
was a gift he received from his mother
was washed away by his daily bath
came upon him in a single sudden moment
C.explanation: "Drop by drop" pictures slow accumulation, so the restlessness built up gradually. A single sudden moment is the opposite. The bath of repentance does not wash it away; he remains restless. The passage traces it to "the teachings of the old Brahmins," not to his mother.

C.prompt: The father's words suggest a conflict between
options: his love for Govinda and his love for his son Siddhartha
his duty to the gods and his duty to the town
his wish to sleep and his wish to pray
his belief in calm speech and the anger he feels
C.explanation: He says "Not proper it is for a Brahmin to speak harsh and angry words. But indignation is in my heart," setting his belief in calm speech against his anger. Govinda is not mentioned. No conflict between gods and town is stated. Sleep and prayer are not what his words weigh against each other.

C.prompt: The parallel endings "With anxiety in his heart" and "With worry in his heart" mainly serve to
options: mark the father's distress growing hour by hour
contrast the father's feelings with Govinda's
show that the father has made his final decision
suggest that Siddhartha shares his father's worry
C.explanation: Each paragraph ends with the father returning to bed troubled, and the echo marks distress continuing through the night. No final decision is made until dawn. Govinda does not appear here. Siddhartha stands "not moving," and his feelings are not described in these lines.

C.prompt: The narrator's description of the Samanas mainly presents them as
options: old men who have given up their search
wealthy pilgrims travelling with servants
gentle teachers welcomed warmly by the whole town
harsh outsiders whose severity still carries a quiet passion
C.explanation: They are "strangers and enemies to the world," marked by "merciless self-denial," yet "a hot scent of quiet passion" follows them, so they are harsh but passionate outsiders. They are lonely, not welcomed. Being "almost naked" rules out wealth. They are "neither old nor young," and nothing suggests they have given up.

C.prompt: How does Passage 2 extend the discontent described in Passage 1?
options: It suggests that even Siddhartha's admired father may share it.
It shows that Siddhartha's discontent has finally ended for good.
It blames Govinda for causing Siddhartha's unrest.
It reveals that Siddhartha's father ordered him to be content.
C.explanation: Passage 1 shows Siddhartha lacking joy; Passage 2 asks whether his father is "also just a searching man, a thirsty man," extending the unrest to him. Neither passage ends the discontent. Govinda is not blamed in either passage. The father gives no order about contentment in Passage 2.

C.prompt: How does Passage 2 develop the bond described in Passage 1?
options: It shows Govinda deciding to break away from Siddhartha.
It shows Govinda sensing that his own fate now follows Siddhartha's.
It shows Govinda becoming a common Brahmin after all.
It shows Siddhartha asking Govinda to come to the forest.
C.explanation: Passage 1 says Govinda wanted to follow Siddhartha; in Passage 2 he senses "his fate is beginning to sprout, and with his, my own." He does not break away. Siddhartha does not invite him; he tells Govinda to speak no more of it. Nothing shows Govinda becoming a common Brahmin.
